Title: Rome in World Time, Part 4: Bread, Blood, and Reform: The Republic Cracks (146–78 BC)

Summary: With no enemy left to fear, Rome turned on itself. Reformers were clubbed to death in the streets, slaves rose in Sicily, Germanic tribes destroyed Roman armies, Italy's allies fought a war for citizenship, a Greek king massacred tens of thousands of Romans in a day, and Sulla marched his army into Rome. Meanwhile Emperor Wu of Han sent Zhang Qian west, opened the Silk Road, and fought his own wars on the steppe in the very same years.

---

Roman writers like Sallust believed the fall of Carthage in 146 BC was the moment Rome began to rot. With no external threat (*metus hostilis*, "fear of the enemy"), the elite turned to greed and feuding. Whether or not that is the whole story, the next 70 years were the most violent in Rome's internal history so far.

## Why the trouble started

- **Land:** wars had flooded Italy with cheap slaves and wealth. The rich bought up small farms and worked them as huge estates (*latifundia*). Small farmers, the backbone of the legions, lost their land.
- **The army:** soldiers had to own property to serve. Fewer property owners meant fewer recruits.
- **The allies:** Italians fought in Rome's wars but had no vote and no protection under Roman law.
- **The provinces:** governors could get rich quickly, and courts made up of senators rarely convicted them.

## Timeline: Rome tears itself apart

| Year (BC) | Event |
|---|---|
| 143–133 | **Numantine War** in Spain. 137: consul Mancinus and 20,000 men surrender; the Senate disowns the deal. 133: Scipio Aemilianus starves Numantia into surrender |
| 135–132 | **First Servile War** in Sicily. A Syrian slave and prophet, **Eunus**, declares himself King Antiochus and leads perhaps tens of thousands |
| 133 | **Tiberius Gracchus**, tribune, passes a land law to give public land to the poor. When he seeks re-election, senators led by Scipio Nasica club him and about 300 followers to death. The first political killing in Rome in centuries |
| 133 | King Attalus III leaves the kingdom of **Pergamum** to Rome in his will |
| 132–129 | **Aristonicus**, claiming the Pergamene throne, raises slaves and the poor in revolt, promising a "City of the Sun" |
| 125 | The Latin colony **Fregellae** revolts and is razed |
| 123–122 | **Gaius Gracchus**, Tiberius' younger brother, passes laws on subsidised grain, land, colonies and courts, and proposes citizenship for the Latins |
| 121 | The Senate passes its first "ultimate decree" (*senatus consultum ultimum*). Consul Opimius attacks; Gaius dies and about 3,000 supporters are killed |
| c. 121–118 | Southern Gaul becomes the province of **Gallia Narbonensis** |
| 113 | The migrating **Cimbri** destroy a Roman army at Noreia |
| 112–105 | **Jugurthine War** in Numidia. Jugurtha bribes Roman senators and supposedly calls Rome "a city for sale" |
| 107 | **Gaius Marius**, a "new man" from Arpinum, is elected consul and recruits landless volunteers |
| 105 | **Arausio**: the Cimbri and Teutones destroy two Roman armies, the worst defeat since Cannae. Jugurtha is captured through a deal arranged by Marius' young officer **Sulla** |
| 104–100 | Marius is consul five years running to face the invaders |
| 104–100 | **Second Servile War** in Sicily under Salvius (called Tryphon) and Athenion |
| 102 | **Aquae Sextiae**: Marius destroys the Teutones |
| 101 | **Vercellae**: Marius and Catulus destroy the Cimbri |
| 100 | Tribune **Saturninus** and his ally Glaucia use violence and murder; the Senate's decree is used again and they are killed. **Julius Caesar** is born (July) |
| 91 | Tribune **Livius Drusus** proposes citizenship for all Italians and is assassinated |
| 91–88 | **Social War**: Rome's Italian allies (*socii*) revolt, form a state called **Italia** with its capital at Corfinium, and mint coins showing the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf |
| 90–89 | Rome wins by giving in: laws grant citizenship to loyal and then to surrendering Italians |
| 89 | Mutinous troops stone their commander, the legate Postumius Albinus. Rome lets it pass |
| 88 | **Mithridates VI** of Pontus orders the killing of Romans and Italians across Asia Minor in a single coordinated massacre, the "Asiatic Vespers" (ancient figures 80,000–150,000) |
| 88 | Sulla is consul and given the Mithridates command; tribune Sulpicius transfers it to Marius. **Sulla marches his army on Rome**, the first time a Roman general did so. Marius flees. The consul Pompeius Rufus is murdered by soldiers he tried to take over |
| 87 | Sulla leaves for Greece. **Cinna** and Marius seize Rome by force and massacre opponents |
| 86 | Marius dies in his seventh consulship. Sulla sacks **Athens** and beats Mithridates at Chaeronea |
| 85 | Peace of Dardanus with Mithridates |
| 84 | Cinna is killed by his own mutinous troops |
| 83–82 | Sulla returns; civil war in Italy. Young **Pompey** raises a private army for him. 82: **Colline Gate**, Sulla wins at the gates of Rome |
| 82–81 | **Proscriptions**: lists of enemies posted in the Forum; anyone could kill them and claim a reward. Sulla becomes dictator, strengthens the Senate, guts the tribunate |
| 80 | **Sertorius**, a Marian general, begins his rebellion in Spain (Part 5) |
| 79 | Sulla resigns and retires |
| 78 | Sulla dies |

## The pattern

Look at what changed between 133 and 82 BC:

- Political violence became normal. Tiberius Gracchus was killed with clubs and benches; by Sulla's time there were mass proscriptions.
- The army changed. Marius took landless volunteers who looked to their general for land when they retired. Their loyalty shifted from the state to the commander.
- Generals discovered that an army could take Rome. Sulla showed the way, and every strongman afterwards followed.
- Italy was unified. After the Social War nearly every free person south of the Po became a Roman citizen.

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**Two empires fighting the steppe in the same years.** In 105–101 BC, Rome was desperately fighting the Cimbri and Teutones, migrating northern peoples, while Han China was sending armies 3,000 km west to Ferghana and fighting the Xiongnu. Both empires reformed their armies under the pressure: Marius' professional volunteers and Emperor Wu's massive cavalry.

**The Silk Road opened as the Gracchi died.** Zhang Qian returned around 126/125 BC with news of Bactria and lands further west. Within a generation, Chinese silk was moving toward the Mediterranean. Romans would be wearing it within a century.

**Tiberius Gracchus' murder and Han's Xiongnu war started in the same year, 133 BC.** In both cases the decision led to decades of consequences, though for China the war was outside and for Rome the war was within.

**A computer was built during the Social War era.** The Antikythera mechanism, a bronze gear-driven model of the heavens, dates to roughly the century covered by this post. Nothing as complex survives from anywhere for the next thousand years.

**Rome and Parthia first met in the 90s BC.** Sulla's meeting with a Parthian envoy on the Euphrates went cordially. Within 40 years their relations would produce one of Rome's worst defeats.

## What comes next

Part 5: Sertorius, Spartacus, Pompey's conquests, Cicero and Catiline, Caesar in Gaul, Crassus' death in Parthia, civil war, the Ides of March, and Actium. Meanwhile Han China sets up the Protectorate of the Western Regions, a Dacian king is assassinated in the same year as Caesar, and the earliest Long Count date in Mesoamerica is carved.

## Sources and notes

- Appian, *Civil Wars*, Book 1. The main continuous narrative from the Gracchi to Sulla.
- Plutarch, *Lives* of Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, Marius and Sulla.
- Sallust, *The Jugurthine War*.
- Diodorus Siculus, Books 34–36 (fragments), for the Sicilian slave wars.
- Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews* 13, for the Hasmoneans.
- Sima Qian, *Shiji*, chapter 123 (Account of Dayuan), for Zhang Qian and Ferghana.
- Mary Beard, *SPQR* (2015), chapters 6–7; Tom Holland, *Rubicon* (2003).
- Overview: [Gracchi (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracchi), [Social War, 91–87 BC (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_War_%2891%E2%80%9387_BC%29), [Sulla's civil war (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulla%27s_civil_war).

**Flags:** The death tolls for the Asiatic Vespers (80,000 to 150,000) come from ancient writers and may be exaggerated. The "Marian reforms" are debated; many historians think Marius' recruitment of the landless continued an existing trend rather than being a single legal reform. The date of the Sulla–Orobazus meeting is disputed (c. 96 or 92 BC). The Antikythera mechanism's construction date is debated, with estimates from about 200 to 60 BC.
